slides.headline: The 'alpha wolf' was a captivity mistake.
slides.sub: Wild packs are families. Even the biologist who spread the idea says so

slides.headline: It began with strangers in a pen
slides.body: Early studies watched unrelated captive wolves thrown together. Those unacquainted adults sorted themselves into alpha, beta and omega ranks. (Pictured: a captive wolf.)

slides.headline: A wild pack is a family
slides.body: Usually a breeding pair and their offspring from the previous 1–3 years. Unrelated wolves are sometimes adopted, but they are the exception.

slides.label: dominance contests Mech saw in 13 summers with a wild pack
slides.body: Watching the same wolf family on Ellesmere Island, Canada, he saw none. The so-called alphas were simply the parents.

slides.headline: The kids leave home
slides.body: Young wolves disperse as early as 9 months; most leave at 1–2 years to find a mate and start their own pack. Few stay past 3.

slides.headline: Time to retire the 'alpha'.
slides.body: Mech's suggested swap: 'breeding male' and 'breeding female', or simply mother and father.
sources: Mech, L.D. (1999) Alpha status, dominance, and division of labor in wolf packs. Can. J. Zool. 77:1196–1203
Mech, L.D.: davemech.org, wolf news and information

caption:
The 'alpha wolf' was a product of captivity: wild gray wolf (Canis lupus) packs are families led by their parents.

The dominance-ladder picture came from studies of unrelated wolves housed together. Wolf biologist L. David Mech compared applying those results to wild packs with studying human family life in a refugee camp. In the wild pack he followed, the mother mostly led pup care and defence, and the father mostly led hunting and travel.

Swipe for what 13 summers with a wild pack showed. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Mech (1999), Canadian Journal of Zoology 77:1196–1203.

Save this for the next time someone brings up 'alpha' behaviour.
